source_text:
καὶ γὰρ ο τε εὐαγγελίζεσθαι ἀπεστάλησαν, ἑαυτοὺς
προσκυνεῖσθαι οὐκ η θελον, ἀλλὰ τὸν αὐτοὺς ἀποστείλαντα Χριστόν. ὁ γὰρ ἐξουσίαν
παρ' αὐτοῦ λαβὼν δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ οὐρανοῦ, ελεγε Κορνηλίῳ ο τι
«ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ανθρωπος», καὶ ἐδίδασκε μὴ ἑαυτὸν προσκυνεῖσθαι ἀλλὰ
τὸν σωτῆρα Χριστόν.
11 περὶ δὲ τῶν ἀγγέλων οἱ πατέρες οἱ ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ συνελθόντες– πάντως γὰρ
οτι διὰ τοιαύτην ὑπόθεσιν συνήχθησαν–λέγουσιν· «ει τις ἐγκαταλείπει τὴν
ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζει, ἀνάθεμα εστω· οτι ἐγκατέλιπε τὸν
κύριον ἡμῶν ̓Ιησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ προσελήλυθε».
orientation: Epiphanius is arguing that neither the apostles nor the angels wish to be worshipped, and he now cites the apostle's words to Cornelius and the Council of Laodicea's anathema against invoking angels.
pass_a_gloss: For indeed [those] who were sent to preach the gospel did not wish themselves to be worshipped, but [wished] the Christ who sent them [to be worshipped]. For the [one] who received authority from him to bind and to loose on earth and in heaven said to Cornelius that "I am a fellow-suffering human like you," and he taught [him] not to worship himself but the Savior Christ. But concerning the angels, the fathers who gathered in Laodicea—for certainly they were gathered because of such a matter—say: "If anyone abandons the church of God and names angels, let him be anathema; because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ and has gone over to idolatry."

choices.english: I am a human being subject to the same feelings as you
choices.why: The adjective ὁμοιοπαθής means sharing the same experiences or feelings; rendering it as 'subject to the same feelings' preserves the compound sense without a hyphenated compound.
rejected: I am a man of like passions with you
I am a fellow-suffering human like you

choices.why: In this context ὀνομάζει means calling upon or invoking angels in worship, not merely naming them; 'invokes' captures the cultic sense.
The perfect προσελήλυθε with the dative means 'has come to' or 'has gone over to'; 'has fallen into' conveys the negative moral sense in natural English.
The glossary requires 'anathema' for ἀνάθεμα; the third-person imperative is rendered with 'let him be'.

bible_refs.note: The apostle's words to Cornelius, 'I myself am also a man,' are echoed in the phrase ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ἄνθρωπος.

pass_b_english: When the apostles were sent out to preach the gospel, they did not want to be worshipped themselves, but only Christ who sent them. The one who received authority from him to bind and loose on earth and in heaven said to Cornelius, "I am a human being of like nature with you," and he taught that he himself was not to be worshipped, but only Christ the Savior.

As for the angels, the fathers who gathered at Laodicea—for they certainly assembled because of just such a matter—say: "If anyone abandons the church of God and invokes angels, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ and has fallen into idolatry."

problems.why: ὁμοιοπαθής means 'of like nature/suffering,' not 'same feelings'; 'fellow human' is the sense.
problems.fix: I am a human being of like nature with you

edits.old: I am a human being subject to the same feelings as you
edits.new: I am a human being of like nature with you

problems.quote: The one who received authority from him to bind and loose on earth and in heaven said to Cornelius
problems.why: Peter is unnamed; reader may not know he holds keys, and Cornelius episode is Acts 10:25-26, not the 'bind and loose' passage.

edits.old: The one who received authority from him to bind and loose on earth and in heaven said to Cornelius,
edits.new: Peter, who received authority from him to bind and loose on earth and in heaven, said to Cornelius,

fixed: The speaker problem is real: the source uses a periphrasis for the apostle, but the English reader may not recognize Peter. Naming him explicitly resolves the ambiguity while keeping the source's description of his authority.

problems.quote: If anyone abandons the church of God and invokes angels, let him be anathema
problems.why: Quoted decree lacks clear attribution marker; reader may think it's Epiphanius speaking.

problems.quote: because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ and has fallen into idolatry
problems.why: The canon's actual wording concerns abandoning Christ for angel-worship; 'fallen into idolatry' may be Epiphanius's gloss.
problems.fix: Clarify whether 'idolatry' is the canon's word or Epiphanius's interpretation.

edits.old: say: "If anyone abandons the church of God and invokes angels, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ and has fallen into idolatry."
edits.new: say: "If anyone abandons the church of God and invokes angels, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ and has gone over to idolatry."

fixed: The source has λέγουσιν introducing the quotation, so the attribution is already clear; no change needed.
The source reads εἰδωλολατρείᾳ προσελήλυθε, which means 'has gone over to idolatry'; the English 'has fallen into idolatry' is close but 'gone over to' better reflects προσελήλυθε, so I adjusted it.

problems.quote: for they certainly assembled because of just such a matter
problems.why: 'certainly' is translator's confidence, not Epiphanius's; Laodicea's canon on angels is not about images.
problems.fix: 'perhaps' or note: 'Epiphanius assumes this was their purpose'.

problems.why: Intro says Laodicea condemned 'angel worship'; the canon text says 'invokes angels'; reader may miss they are the same issue.
problems.fix: Note that 'invoking angels' is the practice the intro calls 'angel worship.'

edits.old: for they certainly assembled because of just such a matter
edits.new: for they assembled because of just such a matter

fixed: Removed 'certainly' from 'for they certainly assembled because of just such a matter': the source πάντως γὰρ ὅτι διὰ τοιαύτην ὑπόθεσιν συνήχθησαν does not express certainty but Epiphanius's assumption; 'for they assembled because of just such a matter' preserves the sense without overstating it.
No edit for 'invokes angels': the source ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζει means 'names/invokes angels,' and the English 'invokes angels' accurately renders it. The glossary note is not a translation problem.

last_rejected.why: ὀνομάζει means 'names' or 'calls upon by name', not 'invokes' in the sense of summoning/invoking; the Laodicean canon targets those who name/appeal to angels as intermediaries, distinct from 'invokes'.
last_rejected.fix: names angels or calls upon angels
last_rejected.ruling: ὀνομάζει can mean 'invoke/call upon by name'; 'invokes' fits the idolatry context and normal semantic range.
